```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(readxl)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

wage_df <- read_excel("C:/Users/dibya/Desktop/Econ 303/Age_HourlyEarnings.xlsx")

age_df <- wage_df[, -1]
ages <- as.numeric(age_df[1, ])
joint <- age_df[-1, ]

p_age <- colSums(joint)
p_age <- p_age / sum(p_age)

age_marginal_tbl <- data.frame(Age = ages, `P(Age)` = as.numeric(p_age))

kable(age_marginal_tbl, digits = 5, caption = "Marginal distribution of Age")


# Empirical Exercise E2.1

## Part A:

# Extract age columns
age_cols <- wage_df[, grepl("^Age|^\\.\\.", names(wage_df))]

# Compute marginal distribution of Age
ages <- as.numeric(age_cols[1, ])
age_probs <- colSums(age_cols[-1, ])
age_marginal <- age_probs / sum(age_probs)

# Display result
data.frame(Age = ages, Probability = age_marginal)

### b) Mean of AHE for each age value (computed + rendered as a table)

```r
```{r}
ahe_vals <- as.numeric(wage_df[[1]][-1])
joint_mat <- as.matrix(joint)

E_AHE_given_Age <- colSums(joint_mat * ahe_vals) / as.numeric(p_age)

cond_mean_tbl <- data.frame(Age = ages, `E(AHE | Age)` = E_AHE_given_Age)

kable(cond_mean_tbl, digits = 4, caption = "Conditional mean of hourly earnings given age")



## Part C:
```r
```{r fig.width=7, fig.height=4}
plot(ages, E_AHE_given_Age,
     pch = 19,
     xlab = "Age",
     ylab = "E[AHE | Age]",
     main = "Mean AHE for each Age vs Age")
lines(ages, E_AHE_given_Age)

## Part D:
```r

Applying the Law of Iterated Expectations,
\[
E(AHE)=\sum_{a} E(AHE \mid \text{Age}=a)\,P(\text{Age}=a).
\]

Using the conditional means and the marginal distribution of Age from the spreadsheet,
\[
E(AHE)=21.5106.
\]

The average hourly wage in the population is ~\$21.51 from the dataset.

## Part E:
The variance of average hourly earnings is given by
\[
\mathrm{Var}(AHE)=E(AHE^2)-[E(AHE)]^2.
\]

\[
\mathrm{Var}(AHE)=164.8203.
\]

The standard deviation of hourly earnings is:
\[
\sigma_{AHE}=\sqrt{164.8203}\approx 12.84.
\]

## Part F:
The covariance between $AHE$ and Age is
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(AHE,\text{Age})=E(AHE\cdot \text{Age})-E(AHE)\,E(\text{Age}).
\]

From the marginal distribution of Age,
\[
E(\text{Age})=29.7663.
\]

\[
\mathrm{Cov}(AHE,\text{Age})=5.7172.
\]

Since the covariance is positive, higher ages tend to be associated with higher hourly earnings.

## Part G:
The correlation between $AHE$ and Age is
\[
\mathrm{Corr}(AHE,\text{Age})
=\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(AHE,\text{Age})}
{\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(AHE)}\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\text{Age})}}.
\]

From
\[
\mathrm{Var}(AHE)=164.8203, 
\qquad 
\mathrm{Var}(\text{Age})=8.1447,
\]
we get
\[
\mathrm{Corr}(AHE,\text{Age})
=\frac{5.7172}{\sqrt{164.8203}\sqrt{8.1447}}
\approx 0.156.
\]


## Part H:
The covariance between age and average hourly earnings is positive, which helps us recognize through data that earnings tend to increase with age among workers aged 25–34. The correlation confirms a positive linear relationship between age and earnings. This relationship is visually supported by the upward-sloping pattern in the plot of conditional mean earnings versus age.
